text: Every data analysis you'll ever write is built from three ideas: storing a value under a name, knowing what kind of value it is, and making decisions or repeating work based on it. If you know T-SQL, you already understand variables, data types, case expressions, and loops of a kind — Python's versions are simpler. There's no declare, no at-sign prefix, and you don't state a type up front. You just assign.

You create a variable by assigning with an equals sign — customer equals the string Ada, orders equals 12, avg underscore order equals 48.5, is underscore active equals True. Calling type on each one shows str, int, float, and bool. Python decides the type from the value you give it, and a variable can be reassigned to a different type later, so it pays to know what each name currently holds.

Arithmetic works as you'd expect, with three division operators worth memorizing. Orders times avg order gives total, 582.0 — notice it's a float, not a plain 582, because multiplying an int by a float produces a float. The forward slash always gives a float; double-slash is floor division, dropping the remainder; percent gives the remainder. Strings build cleanly with an f-string — an f before the quote, with curly braces holding an expression and an optional format, like colon dot 2 f for two decimal places, which you'll use constantly when reporting money.

None is Python's way of saying no value here, similar to NULL in SQL — test for it with is None, not a double-equals. Python also treats some values as false in conditions: 0, an empty string, an empty list, and None itself. Everything else counts as true, so bool of zero, bool of an empty string, and bool of an empty list are all False, while bool of any non-empty string is True.

An if statement runs a block only when a condition holds, and that block is defined by indentation — four spaces by convention, not by braces. Check if total is greater than 500 for gold, elif greater than 200 for silver, else bronze. Python checks top to bottom and runs the first true condition — with total at 582, that assigns gold. This is the Python cousin of a T-SQL CASE WHEN expression.

A for loop walks through a collection one item at a time. Loop over a list of totals, adding each one to a running total and printing both as you go — you'd see 20 then 20, 55.5 then 75.5, 130 then 205.5. When you also need the position, wrap the collection in enumerate, which gives you index-item pairs. The range function generates a sequence of numbers, and a while loop repeats as long as a condition stays true. Break exits a loop immediately; continue skips to the next item.

Two gotchas worth knowing now. Floats are stored in binary, so 0.1 plus 0.2 does not equal 0.3 exactly — never compare floats with a double-equals; round first, like round of 0.1 plus 0.2 to 2 places, which does equal 0.3. And a plus sign on two strings concatenates them rather than adding numbers — string 5 plus string 5 gives 55, not 10 — exactly the bug you get when a number column is read in as text. Convert with int or float first.

To recap: assign with equals, check types with type, branch with if, elif, and else, and loop with for and while, letting indentation define every block. Watch for float comparisons and string-versus-number mix-ups — they're everywhere in real data. Next lesson: functions and comprehensions.
